title: Quiz: Acceptance Sampling Plans and OC Curves

questions.text: A single sampling plan has n=50, c=1. A batch of 500 items is inspected. What happens if 3 defectives are found in the sample?
options: Accept the lot — 3 defectives out of 500 is acceptable
Accept the lot — 3 out of 50 is within the AQL
questions.explanation: The decision rule is: if the number of defectives d > c, reject the lot. Here d=3 > c=1, so the lot is rejected regardless of the lot size.

questions.text: Producer's risk (α) is the probability of:
options: Accepting a bad lot (Type II error)
Rejecting a good lot (Type I error)
The sample size being too small
questions.explanation: Producer's risk (α) is the probability of rejecting a lot that is actually good quality (at or better than the AQL). It is a Type I error — rejecting a true null hypothesis.

questions.text: A steeper OC curve means the sampling plan is better at discriminating between good and bad lots.
questions.explanation: A steep OC curve means Pa drops sharply as p increases past the AQL. This means the plan reliably accepts good lots and reliably rejects bad ones. An ideal OC curve would be a vertical line at the AQL.

questions.text: LTPD (Lot Tolerance Percent Defective) is the quality level at which:
options: The producer considers the lot to be of acceptable quality
The consumer considers the lot to be unacceptably bad
The process is declared out of control
questions.explanation: LTPD is the quality level that the consumer (buyer) considers unacceptable. At the LTPD, the probability of accepting the lot should be low (equal to the consumer's risk β).

questions.text: Acceptance sampling can be used to improve process quality by identifying and removing defects.
questions.explanation: Acceptance sampling only makes accept/reject decisions on batches — it does not improve the process. SPC and DMAIC are the tools for process improvement. Acceptance sampling is a form of inspection, not improvement.
